title: π, τ and κ without a puff of air
learn: Learn π, τ and κ without the puff

text.american: When an English word starts with p, t or k, a puff of air follows it: hold your hand in front of your mouth and say “pin”, “tin”, “kin”. Greek π, τ and κ never have that puff. And between two vowels an American t goes soft, almost a d, as in “water” and “city”; a Greek τ never does. Long ago the puff was what made φ, θ and χ, so to a Greek ear it is a foreign accent.
text.british: When an English word starts with p, t or k, a puff of air follows it: hold your hand in front of your mouth and say “pin”, “tin”, “kin”. Greek π, τ and κ never have that puff. Nor is a Greek τ ever swallowed into a catch in the throat, as many British speakers say the t of “water” and “bottle”. Long ago the puff was what made φ, θ and χ, so to a Greek ear it is a foreign accent.

steps.text: You already say them without the puff: after an s. Hold your hand in front of your mouth and say “spin”, “stop” and “skate”: no puff. Say “spin”, then drop the s and keep the p just as it was: that is π. Do the same with “stop” for τ and “skate” for κ.
Listen: no breath follows π in πατήρ, τ in τέκνα, or κ in κόσμος. To an English ear they can sound a little like b, d and g; they are only clean, short and dry. In ὅτι the τ stays a full t.

Each pair differs only in π and φ, τ and θ, or κ and χ. Today φ is f, θ the th of “thin” and χ the throaty ch; so keep the puff off π, τ and κ, and they never drift toward them. Hear both words, then say both.

text.american: Say each word after the voice, with your hand in front of your mouth: you should feel no puff. In ὅτι keep the τ a real t, not the soft d of “city”.
text.british: Say each word after the voice, with your hand in front of your mouth: you should feel no puff. In ὅτι say the τ right through, with no catch in the throat.

steps.text: This verse is full of π, τ and κ, each marked. Hear it, then say it with your hand in front of your mouth: no puff on any of them, in περιπατεῖ least of all.
